column4: The ayah states the section's division almost verbatim: “عَلَيْكَ ٱلْبَلَاغُ وَعَلَيْنَا ٱلْحِسَابُ”; delivery belongs to the Messenger and reckoning to God.
“وَمَا أَنتَ عَلَيْهِم بِجَبَّارٍ” denies the Prophet coercive mastery, then “فَذَكِّرْ بِٱلْقُرْءَانِ” assigns him reminder for one who fears the warning.
The ayah expressly says the Prophet was not sent as their guardian and that only conveyance is upon him, matching both halves of the section's limit.
God says He made the Prophet neither a guardian over the rejecters nor their agent, a direct parallel to “not a musayṭir over them.”
God alone may show mercy or punish, while the Prophet was not sent as the people's agent; it directly assigns punishment and oversight away from him.
“أَفَأَنتَ تُكْرِهُ ٱلنَّاسَ” asks whether the Prophet would compel people into faith, directly exposing the coercion excluded by the reminder's office.
The only other Quranic مُصَيْطِرُون asks whether the rejecters possess the Lord's treasuries or are themselves the controllers, denying them the mastery denied to the Prophet.
“وَكُلُّ صَغِيرٍ وَكَبِيرٍ مُّسْتَطَرٌ” uses the section's س ط ر root for every small and great thing entered in lines, locating the comprehensive record with God.
“فَذَكِّرْ إِن نَّفَعَتِ ٱلذِّكْرَىٰ” gives the same command to remind and begins the exact response-and-judgment sequence invoked by the section.
The one who fears will receive the reminder, matching the receptive addressee in 50:45 and supplying the first response in the sequence begun at 87:9.
The most wretched avoids the reminder, paralleling the person who turns away in 88:23 and moving the neighbouring sequence from reminder to refusal.
The refuser enters “ٱلنَّارَ ٱلْكُبْرَىٰ,” the greatest fire, a direct counterpart to the greatest punishment that God administers in 88:24.
“وَذَكِّرْ فَإِنَّ ٱلذِّكْرَىٰ تَنفَعُ ٱلْمُؤْمِنِينَ” repeats the command and identifies those who benefit rather than making the Prophet responsible for all responses.
“كَلَّا إِنَّهَا تَذْكِرَةٌ” names the revelation itself as a reminder, the instrument by which something is brought back to mind in the source definition.
“فَمَن شَآءَ ذَكَرَهُۥ” leaves taking the reminder to the willing hearer, marking the same boundary between reminding and controlling response.
Moses and Aaron say revelation has declared that punishment falls upon “مَن كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ”; denial, turning away, and divine punishment form the same sequence as 88:23–24.
“If they turn away” is answered by “فَإِنَّمَا عَلَيْكَ ٱلْبَلَاغُ,” joining the source's turning-away verb to the Messenger's strictly bounded duty.
After “فَإِن تَوَلَّيْتُمْ,” the hearers are told that only clear conveyance rests on God's Messenger, the section's role division in one conditional sentence.
“If they turn away, only clear conveyance is upon you” directly pairs refusal with the Prophet's noncoercive task.
The ayah again makes turning away the hearers' act and clear conveyance the Messenger's sole obligation.
“وَمَن تَوَلَّىٰ” is followed by God's statement that the Prophet was not sent as a guardian over them, combining the same refusal with the same denied office.
When the Prophet's people deny the truth, he must say “لَّسْتُ عَلَيْكُم بِوَكِيلٍ,” a close first-person counterpart to “لست عليهم بمصيطر.”
Seeing or remaining blind benefits or harms each person, and the Prophet says he is not their guardian; response is personal rather than enforced by him.
Guidance benefits oneself and error falls upon oneself, while the Prophet is not an agent over the hearers, precisely separating proclamation from outcome.
After the Book is sent for humankind, guidance or error belongs to each soul and the Prophet is explicitly not their agent.
God is guardian over those who take patrons besides Him, while the Prophet is not their agent; the ayah assigns the supervisory office to its true holder.
“The Messenger has only conveyance,” while God knows what people disclose and conceal, dividing public proclamation from comprehensive oversight.
The Messenger bears what he was charged with and the hearers bear what they were charged with; his only duty is clear conveyance, a precise allocation of responsibility.
Denial does not enlarge a messenger's authority: the ayah says that only clear conveyance rests on the Messenger.
The town's messengers answer rejection with “وَمَا عَلَيْنَآ إِلَّا ٱلْبَلَاغُ ٱلْمُبِينُ,” giving the same stance beyond Muhammad's own address.
The polytheists use divine will to excuse their worship, but the ayah asks whether messengers have any task beyond clear conveyance; it distinguishes God's power from their commission.
“لَّيْسَ عَلَيْكَ هُدَىٰهُمْ” removes responsibility for making people guided from the Prophet and assigns guidance to God.
“لَيْسَ لَكَ مِنَ ٱلْأَمْرِ شَىْءٌ” excludes the Prophet from deciding whether God accepts or punishes wrongdoers, matching the section's ownership of punishment.
The Prophet cannot guide even one he loves; God guides whom He wills, defining the practical limit of reminder.
Hud says he has conveyed what he was sent with even if his people turn away, while his Lord succeeds them and guards all things.
Noah says “إِنْ حِسَابُهُمْ إِلَّا عَلَىٰ رَبِّى,” an exact prophetic declaration that other people's reckoning rests only with the Lord.
Noah concludes “إِنْ أَنَا۠ إِلَّا نَذِيرٌ مُّبِينٌ,” pairing his limited warning role with the divine account stated in 26:113.
The Prophet has none of the believers' account upon him and they have none of his; he may not act as judge by driving them away.
Those who convey God's messages fear none but Him, and “كَفَىٰ بِٱللَّهِ حَسِيبًا” identifies God as the sufficient reckoner.
“We did not send the Quran down to you that you should suffer” removes an impossible burden from the Prophet before 20:3 states its actual function.
The Quran is “تَذْكِرَةً لِّمَن يَخْشَىٰ,” a reminder for one who fears, closely matching both 88:21 and the audience specified in 50:45.
The Prophet can warn the one who follows the Reminder and fears the Merciful unseen; the wording limits the effective audience without making him control it.
“إِنَّمَآ أَنتَ مُنذِرُ مَن يَخْشَىٰهَا” uses the same restrictive stance: he is only a warner to one who fears the Hour.
The Prophet disclaims power even over benefit or harm to himself and says he is only a warner and bearer of good news, ruling out the master's power implicit in musayṭir.
The Prophet is only a warner while God is agent over everything, directly distributing the two roles the section distinguishes.
The Prophet is commanded to say he possesses neither harm nor right direction for the hearers, a direct denial of controlling power.
He cannot protect even himself from God and has no refuge apart from Him, sharpening the absence of delegated mastery stated in 72:21.
His exception is conveyance of God's messages; disobedience then meets God's enduring fire, joining limited mission to divine punishment.
The truth is announced from the Lord, belief or disbelief is left to the hearer, and God has prepared the wrongdoers' fire; proclamation and punishment remain distinct.
A person is reminded by the Lord's signs and then turns away; God, not the reminder, exacts vengeance from the guilty.
Whoever turns away from the Lord's remembrance is led by Him into mounting punishment, directly joining refusal of remembrance to divine requital.
Only the most wretched enters the blazing fire, beginning a close parallel to the 87 and 88 sequences.
“ٱلَّذِى كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ” identifies that fire's person by the same denial and turning away as 88:23.
The ayah isolates the case “إِن كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ,” the same paired human response that precedes punishment in the source image.
“أَلَمْ يَعْلَم بِأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَرَىٰ” answers denial and turning with God's sight, locating the true oversight with God.
“فَمَا لَهُمْ عَنِ ٱلتَّذْكِرَةِ مُعْرِضِينَ” stages people actively turning away from the reminder itself.
“كَلَّآ إِنَّهُۥ تَذْكِرَةٌ” repeats the identification of revelation as the reminder after the scene of aversion.
“فَمَن شَآءَ ذَكَرَهُۥ” makes remembering the hearer's chosen response rather than an act forced by the Messenger.
Their willing does not escape God's will, and He alone is worthy of fear and forgiveness; this qualifies freedom of response without transferring control to the Prophet.
The Prophet is told to turn away from the rejecters and is not blameworthy, immediately before being told still to remind in 51:55.
“فَذَكِّرْ” remains the Prophet's act despite accusations that he is a soothsayer or madman; rejection changes neither his task nor his authority.
The Prophet is told to turn aside from one who has turned from God's remembrance and wants only the nearer life, bounding his pursuit of the refuser.
Most people will not believe however intensely the Prophet desires it, exposing the limit that makes reminder rather than control his task.
He asks no payment, and the message is only “ذِكْرٌ لِّلْعَٰلَمِينَ,” completing the contrast between his desire and his assigned means.
“وَكُلُّ شَىْءٍ فَعَلُوهُ فِى ٱلزُّبُرِ” identifies deeds as the contents of the records whose lined inscription is stated in 54:53.
The oath by the pen and “مَا يَسْطُرُونَ” presents the source root's basic act of putting things into written lines.
“وَكِتَٰبٍ مَّسْطُورٍ” gives the same س ط ر sense as an inscribed book, near the surah's later challenge about who the controllers are.
The open parchment supplies the surface on which the neighbouring “inscribed book” is set out in lines.
“وَإِنَّ عَلَيْكُمْ لَحَٰفِظِينَ” names actual guardians over people, the office explicitly denied to the Prophet.
Those guardians are “كِرَامًا كَٰتِبِينَ,” joining watching to writing exactly as the source definition of musayṭir does.
The guardian-scribes know what people do, completing the supervisory scene while distinguishing its agents from the Messenger.
God hears secret speech and His messengers beside the speakers write it down, supplying the true unseen surveillance and record.
The two receivers seated to right and left receive each person's deeds, staging the assigned recorders rather than prophetic supervision.
No word is uttered without an attendant observer ready to record it, the concrete watcher-writer behind the section's dictionary image.
God says “وَنَكْتُبُ مَا قَدَّمُوا۟ وَءَاثَٰرَهُمْ” and counts everything in a clear register, expressly assigning the record to “We.”
God's book speaks against people in truth because “إِنَّا كُنَّا نَسْتَنسِخُ مَا كُنتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ,” making their works the copied record used in judgment.
The placed record omits neither small nor great and people find their deeds present, closely unfolding 54:53's “small and great inscribed.”
Each person's record is brought out on resurrection as an open book, turning the hidden supervision into a personally encountered document.
“Read your book” makes the person sufficient as a reckoner against himself that day; God's accounting is disclosed through the written record rather than delegated to the Prophet.
When opponents secretly plot at night, “وَٱللَّهُ يَكْتُبُ مَا يُبَيِّتُونَ”; the Prophet turns aside and relies on God, joining divine recording to prophetic noncontrol.
God is witness while any deed is done, and nothing escapes Him or the clear record; the comprehensive oversight belongs to Him.
God has counted deeds people themselves forgot and is witness over everything, directly grounding the final account in divine preservation.
God is the irresistible master over His servants and sends guardians until death, locating authority and watching under His command.
After death people are returned to Allah, their true Master; judgment is His and He is swiftest in reckoning, closely combining 88:25–26.
People are presented before their Lord “صَفًّا” for judgment; the source's image of things put in rows meets return and account in one scene.
A city's destruction or severe punishment before resurrection is “فِى ٱلْكِتَٰبِ مَسْطُورًا,” joining lined inscription to punishment administered by God.

The source dictionary says تَوَلَّى can mean taking office as well as turning away; in “وَإِذَا تَوَلَّىٰ” the man turns away or gains power and then corrupts the land, making that double hearing consequential.
The rebuke asks whether the approaching man might purify himself, showing that the result of the encounter remains a possibility rather than the Prophet's possession.
The man may remember and have the reminder benefit him, stating the causal reach of reminder without guaranteeing response.
The Prophet attends to the self-satisfied person, beginning the correction of how he distributes his finite attention as a reminder.
“You attend to him” identifies the Prophet's mistaken prioritization, which the reminder scene then reverses.
The Prophet is not responsible if the self-satisfied hearer does not purify himself, a direct limit on responsibility for response.
The other hearer comes striving, supplying the willing approach to reminder that contrasts with turning away.
That seeker fears, matching the section's recurring description of the person for whom warning and reminder work.
The Prophet is distracted from the fearful seeker, the specific error corrected before revelation is named a reminder in 80:11.
“No compulsion in religion” states the general boundary corresponding to the Prophet's lack of coercive mastery, while grounding response in the distinction between guidance and error.
Jesus says he was a witness while among his people, but after God took him, “كُنتَ أَنتَ ٱلرَّقِيبَ عَلَيْهِمْ”; witness and ultimate watcher are sharply distinguished.

God, His Messenger, and believers will see people's outward work, but people then return to the Knower of seen and unseen who tells them what they did; prophetic seeing stops short of comprehensive account.
Joseph asks to be appointed over the land's storehouses as a knowing guardian, a legitimate, specifically granted stewardship that marks the boundary around the ungranted mastery in 52:37 and 88:22.
The servants of the Merciful do not respond to reminders by falling deaf and blind; their receptive posture reverses the turning away developed in the source.
God sends the Prophet as witness, bearer of good news, and warner; these positive commissions clarify that denying musayṭir authority does not erase every public role.
At judgment the Prophet is brought as a witness over his community, a defined evidentiary role distinct from controlling them or owning their account.
On the day no soul controls anything for another and “ٱلْأَمْرُ يَوْمَئِذٍ لِّلَّهِ,” all creaturely mastery gives way to God's exclusive command.
The angels say “وَإِنَّا لَنَحْنُ ٱلصَّآفُّونَ,” an animate heavenly rank that carries the source's row image beyond cushions and written lines.
Those same ranked angels glorify God; ordered rows here serve worship, distinguishing another hand and purpose behind arrangement.
The neighbour explains that the entrant into the greatest fire neither dies nor lives, extending the punishment invoked by the section beyond the shared “greatest” wording.
The Prophet disclaims possession of God's treasuries and knowledge of the unseen and says he only follows revelation, complementing 52:37's treasury-and-control challenge.
Noah likewise says he does not possess God's treasuries or know the unseen, showing another messenger refusing the master's resources and knowledge.
The rejecters are asked whether they hold the treasuries of their mighty, giving Lord, a close treasury challenge to 52:37 without its musayṭir word.
God says every thing's treasuries are with “Us” and it descends only in a known measure, positively locating the stores whose possession 52:37 denies to people.
“I am Allah; there is no god but Me, so worship Me ... for My remembrance” joins the source definition of Allah as the worshipped one to ذِكْر.
Every messenger receives the same revelation that there is no god but God and that He alone is to be worshipped, connecting messenger commission to the source's definition of Allah's name.
The revelation is a reminder and whoever wills may take a path to the Lord, another formulation of offered recollection rather than compelled response.
“This is a reminder; whoever wills may take a path to his Lord” repeats the hearer's willing response to revelation.
Human willing remains within God's will, a neighbouring qualification that prevents noncoercion from being mistaken for independence from God.
The Quran is nothing but a reminder to the worlds, identifying the message by the same function assigned to its bearer.
The reminder addresses whoever wills to go straight, placing response with the hearer.
The hearer's will depends on the will of Allah, Lord of the worlds, completing the boundary around human response.
God has made the Quran easy for remembrance and asks whether anyone will take heed; its repeated refrain enacts the source definition of zikrā as abundant repetition.
The same invitation to remember is repeated after a second warning narrative, making recurrence itself part of the reminder.
The refrain returns after another destroyed people, again offering remembrance without compelling it.
Its fourth occurrence completes the surah's sustained repetition of the invitation to take reminder.
God says He has repeatedly varied matters in the Quran so people might remember, yet the repetition can increase their aversion; reminder does not control reception.
God sets out every kind of example in the Quran so that people may remember, describing the repeated means rather than a guaranteed outcome.
The Arabic Quran repeatedly varies warnings so people may become mindful or the text may produce remembrance in them.
When the Prophet mentions his Lord alone in the Quran, the hearers turn their backs in aversion, physically staging the source sense of تَوَلَّى as turning away.
The Prophet must warn that if the people turn away he fears for them a great day's punishment; he announces the danger rather than administering it.
If the hearers turn away, the Prophet's response is to say he has warned them of a thunderbolt, keeping his act verbal while judgment remains God's.
If the people turn away, the Prophet says he has informed them equally and does not know when the promise will arrive, combining conveyance with lack of control over its fulfillment.
The Bedouins may obey and receive good reward or turn away and be punished by God; their choice and God's requital mirror the section's division.
Whoever opposes the Messenger is left to what he has taken up—“نُوَلِّهِۦ مَا تَوَلَّىٰ”—and then brought to hell, giving the source's undertakes-for-himself nuance a punitive outcome.
Whoever turns away from God's remembrance receives a constricted life and is raised blind, a concrete consequence of refusing remembrance.
God explains that His signs came and were forgotten, so the refuser is forgotten that day; judgment answers the earlier rejection of remembrance.
“وَلَٰكِن كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ” repeats the paired denial and turning away of 88:23 in another judgment passage.
At judgment the Spirit and angels stand in a row and speak only by the Merciful's permission, joining ordered ranks to exclusive divine authority.
The angels come “صَفًّا صَفًّا” at the final judgment, another meeting of arrangement in rows with the account scene.
Rejecters call the revelation old written tales and claim the Prophet had them written and dictated; their false account turns the root's writing image against the reminder itself.
God sets just balances for resurrection and brings even a mustard seed to account, concretely expressing the exact reckoning that rests on Him.
Every soul is repaid for what it earned, without injustice, and Allah is swift in account; this states the divine execution of the section's assigned reckoning.
Immediately after 13:40's role division, God is said to judge with none able to reverse His judgment and to be swift in reckoning.
The Prophet “frowned and turned away,” using the section's تَوَلَّى scene inside the very passage that will identify revelation as a reminder.
The blind seeker coming to the Prophet identifies the person from whom he turned in 80:1 and anchors the correction of how a reminder meets its hearer.
The reminder of 80:11 is located in honored pages, bringing the offered recollection into a written object.
Those pages are raised and purified, continuing the material setting of the reminder introduced in 80:13.
The pages are “by the hands of scribes,” naming a proper writing hand immediately after the reminder passage, just as the section distinguishes its writer from the Prophet.
The scribes are noble and righteous, completing the neighbouring identification of the hands that carry the written reminder.
Those who are mindful bear none of the mockers' account; their responsibility is only a reminder, directly bringing ذِكْرَى and another person's reckoning into one boundary.
The Prophet is told to remind with the Quran lest a soul be held for what it earned; reminder precedes a divine account where no patron or intercessor can replace God.
Shuayb tells his people that he is not a guardian over them, another messenger explicitly refusing the office described by musayṭir.
After a person takes desire as his god, the Prophet is asked whether he can be an agent over him; the object of worship and the denied supervisory role meet in one challenge.
Noah asks what knowledge he has of what his followers used to do, disclaiming the inspection of their deeds just before assigning their account to his Lord in 26:113.
The Prophet says he only follows what is revealed and is only a clear warner, sharply limiting both his initiative and his commission.
Knowledge of the promised judgment is only with Allah, while the Prophet is only a clear warner; knowledge and warning are allotted to different speakers.
The Prophet is only a warner, while Allah is the sole deity and overwhelming One, coupling his limited office with God's unique authority.
“You are only a warner” is a direct restrictive formulation of the same prophetic task boundary.
The hearers are asked to reflect that their companion is no madman but only a clear warner, defining his role amid their rejection.
Signs are with Allah and the Prophet is only a clear warner, separating divine possession of proof from his verbal commission.
The Prophet is commanded to tell all people that he is only a clear warner to them, another direct self-description bounded by إِنَّمَا.
The Prophet offers one admonition and is described as only a warner before severe punishment, joining a concentrated reminder to a punishment he does not execute.
The Quran is a proclamation for people so they may be warned, know that God is one, and remember; conveyance, sole worship, and recollection converge without coercion.
Every community received a messenger with the charge to worship Allah and avoid false powers; the universal message identifies the worshipped One without giving messengers His authority.
Joseph contrasts scattered lords with Allah, the One and Overpowering, directly testing the source definition of musayṭirūn as masters against the true sovereign.
Judgment belongs only to Allah, who commanded that none but He be worshipped; exclusive account and the source definition of Allah as the worshipped One are stated together.
The Prophet may nearly destroy himself because people do not believe, revealing the emotional burden that the limit on his responsibility relieves.
God could send a sign that made their necks remain submissive, showing that compelling submission lies in divine power rather than the Prophet's reminder.
However eager the Prophet is for their guidance, guidance is not his to produce; his concern cannot turn proclamation into control.
The Prophet is warned that he may consume himself with grief if people do not believe this discourse, another direct correction of responsibility for response.
The Prophet must not grieve over disbelief; the disbelievers return to “Us,” who will tell them their deeds and know what hearts contain.
Whether God shows the Prophet some promised punishment or takes him first, the people return to “Us” and God witnesses what they do, closely repeating 13:40's frame.
Whether the Prophet sees part of what is promised or dies first, the people are returned to “Us”; fulfillment and return remain God's affair.
If God takes the Prophet away, “We” will exact retribution from the rejecters, explicitly removing punishment from the Prophet's hand.
If God instead shows him what they were promised, God remains fully powerful over them; either branch keeps enforcement divine.
God tells the Prophet to leave the comfortable deniers to Him and grant them a little respite, a vivid handoff of the rejecters' case.
“Leave Me with the one I created alone” assigns dealing with the rejecting opponent directly to God.
God tells the Prophet to leave to Him whoever denies this discourse, then promises a hidden divine process of requital.
The Prophet must proclaim what he is commanded and turn away from the associators, combining outspoken delivery with disengagement from control.
“We suffice you against the mockers” supplies the divine action paired with the Prophet's proclamation in 15:94.
The message comes as good news and warning, yet most people turn away and do not hear; their refusal remains distinct from the messenger's act.
Those who disbelieve turn away from what they were warned of, restaging refusal after warning without making the warner its enforcer.
The keepers of hell ask each arriving group whether a warner came, placing human warning before divine punishment and naming different agents at each stage.
The condemned admit that a warner came and that they denied him, confirming rejection rather than failed coercion as the path to punishment.
The Prophet is told to turn away from the rejecters while the divine caller summons them to the dreadful event, handing the scene from reminder to judgment.
The humbled dead emerge from graves like scattered locusts, supplying the returned people in the judgment scene opened by 54:6.
They hasten to the caller and name it a hard day, completing the consequence toward which the Prophet was told simply to step aside.
Pharaoh denies and disobeys the warning, beginning another refusal-and-punishment sequence parallel to 88:23–24.
He then turns his back and strives, making the physical act behind تَوَلَّى explicit.
Pharaoh claims to be the people's highest lord, embodying the false human mastery that the section denies.
Allah seizes that claimant in punishment for the latter and former offense, restoring punishment and mastery to God.
Guidance or error falls on each soul, no bearer carries another's burden, and God does not punish until He sends a messenger; message and account are carefully apportioned.
No burdened soul bears another's burden, and the Prophet effectively warns those who fear unseen; purification benefits the person who undertakes it.
For some hearers, warning or not warning is equal because they will not believe, setting the limit that makes 36:11 specify the receptive audience.
The Book is sent so the Prophet may warn by it and as a reminder to believers, defining the revealed instrument and its two verbal functions.
The Quran is a blessed reminder sent down by God, and the hearers are asked whether they will deny it; reminder and denial face one another directly.
A truthful book is with God and speaks the truth about people without injustice, identifying the record that serves divine account.
“We enumerated everything in a book” assigns exhaustive recording to the divine speaker and gives the section's line-by-line image a comprehensive object.
The wicked have a record in Sijjin, beginning a judgment passage in which their deeds are fixed in writing.
That record is “a book inscribed,” the concrete written form of the wicked person's account.
The righteous likewise have a record in Illiyyin, showing that comprehensive recording covers the opposite outcome too.
The righteous record too is “a book inscribed,” repeating the fixed written account across both groups.
Those brought near witness the righteous record, distinguishing witnesses to the account from its divine owner.
The person given his book in his right hand invites others to read it, staging the record as publicly available evidence.
He says he was certain he would meet his account, linking the readable book in 69:19 to reckoning.
The person given his book in his left hand wishes he had never received it, reversing the right-hand record scene.
He wishes he had never known his account, identifying the feared meaning of the book received in 69:25.
Receiving one's book in the right hand begins the favourable form of the final account.
That person will be reckoned with an easy reckoning, an explicit instance of the ح س ب outcome that belongs to God.
Receiving the book behind one's back supplies the contrary record scene.
The recipient of that record calls for destruction, the immediate response to the unfavourable account.
He enters a blazing fire, completing the movement from written account to divinely administered punishment.
People emerge separately so that they may be shown their deeds, joining return to the disclosure of the record's contents.
Even an atom's weight of good is seen, specifying the small deed covered by 54:53's comprehensive inscription.
Even an atom's weight of evil is seen, completing the record's exactness on the other side.
At judgment the book is set down and prophets and witnesses are brought while God judges in truth, locating each participant without confusing witness with judge.
Every soul is paid in full for what it did and God knows their deeds best, completing the account scene of 39:69.
All in heaven and earth belongs to Allah; when people return to Him, He tells them what they did because He knows everything.
“To your Lord is the return” supplies the destination behind God's sight in 96:14 and the denier's turning in 96:13.
The Prophet declares our deeds are ours and yours are yours; God will gather everyone and to Him is the destination, separating responsibility before reunion.
The question denies that humans were created pointlessly or would not be returned to “Us,” making return essential to accountable creation.
Allah is exalted as the true King and sole deity, identifying the sovereign to whom the return in 23:115 belongs.
God is Master of the Day of Recompense, the most compact statement of who owns the final account.
Allah repays every soul for what it earned and is swift in reckoning, stating both the subject and execution of the account.
The disbeliever reaches what seemed like water and instead finds Allah, who pays his account in full; the image makes divine reckoning the unavoidable end.
Every soul has a guardian over it, affirming real supervision while leaving the section's denial that the Prophet is that guardian intact.
When Allah alone was invoked people disbelieved, but accepted partners; the ayah concludes that judgment belongs to Allah, the Most High and Great.
On the day all are exposed, God asks whose kingdom it is and answers that it belongs to Allah alone, excluding every rival master.
Each soul earns only against itself, none bears another's burden, and all return to their Lord for disclosure of their disputes.
Disbelief or gratitude belongs to the person, no bearer carries another's burden, and the return to the Lord ends in disclosure of deeds.
The Prophet is told to turn aside from the hypocrites yet admonish them with penetrating speech, showing that disengagement from control can coexist with continued verbal reminder.
The Prophet must command what is right and turn away from the ignorant, a stance that combines instruction with refusal to dominate the resistant.
The Prophet is told to pardon the rejecters and say peace, while their eventual knowing remains future; his immediate posture is separated from judgment.
The person who purifies himself succeeds, providing the positive hearer-side result after the reminder and greatest-fire sequence.
He remembers his Lord's name and prays, continuing the receptive alternative to avoidance of the reminder.
The revelation is nothing but a reminder to the worlds, another restrictive identification of the message's function.
The Quran is only a reminder to the worlds despite the rejecters' hostile accusation, preserving its function under opposition.
The Prophet asks no reward except that whoever wills take a path to the Lord, making freely chosen response the only requested return for his mission.
